title: Gardeners of literature
takeaway: Good people keep spreading their 'fragrance' long after they're gone.
scene: An untitled verse that seems to remember a writer friend, perhaps Naseem (whose name means 'breeze'), who looked after the 'garden' of poetry.

original: گلشن وچہ اوہ پھل نویکلے سن
transliteration: Gulshan vich oh phull naveekle san
translation: In the garden there were some rare, unique flowers
that always went on spreading their fragrance.
couplets.story: In the garden of poetry there were a few special flowers, people who were one of a kind. They kept spreading their sweet smell everywhere.

original: مالی سن اوہ ادب دے بوٹیاں دے
ہر ہر غنچے دی پلک سنواردے رہے
transliteration: Maali san oh adab de bootiyaan de
Har har ghunche di palak sanvaarde rahe
translation: They were gardeners of the plants of literature,
tending even the eyelashes of every single bud.
couplets.story: They looked after literature like gardeners looking after plants. They cared for every little bud, even the smallest details.

original: قوم وطن دے غم نوں سمجھ اپنا
دل تے ظلم دے تیر سہاردے رہے
transliteration: Qaum vatan de gham nu samajh apna
Dil te zulm de teer sahaarde rahe
translation: Treating the nation's and homeland's sorrow as their own,
they kept taking the arrows of injustice on their hearts.
couplets.story: They felt the country's pain as if it were their own, and they took a lot of unfairness without giving up.

original: ہم باد نسیم دے وانگ احمدؔ
علم و فن دے جوہر نکھاردے رہے
translation: Like the gentle morning breeze, Ahmad,
they kept bringing out the best in learning and art.
couplets.story: Like a gentle breeze, they kept helping knowledge and art shine.

why: A gentle tribute to the people who quietly look after culture and help others grow.
prompt: Who are the 'gardeners' in your life, the people who help others grow without needing credit?
notes: Untitled; begins at the bottom of page 96 and ends at the top of page 97. 'Baad-e-naseem' (gentle breeze) may be a nod to Sheikh Iftikhar Ahmad Naseem (page 74).
